extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning real analysis / sequences and limits
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and standard techniques about sequences of real numbers: decimal representations, boundedness, convergence (epsilon–M), monotone sequences, tails/subsequences, squeeze lemma, algebra of limits, roots/absolute value, and recursively defined sequences (Newton method example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1.5.3 — Rational numbers have eventually repeating decimal expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is rational and x = p/q (p,q positive integers, unique representation assumed), then the decimal digits of x eventually start repeating: there exist positive integers N and P such that for all n ≥ N, d_n = d_{n+P}. The period P is at most q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via long division: remainders when repeatedly multiplying by 10 are at most q so must repeat after ≤ q steps; uniqueness caveat for numbers with two decimal representations (e.g., 0.4999... = 0.5) is noted. The converse (eventually repeating ⇒ rational) is left as an exercise. Example consequences: a constructed decimal whose digits never repeat is irrational; exercise asks to generalize to base b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 1.5.4 — Explicit irrational by nonrepeating digit pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: The decimal x = 0.101001000100001000001... (n zeros then a 1, for growing n) is irrational because its digits never eventually repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Proposition 1.5.3: for every candidate period P, further along the expansion you see a 1 followed by at least P zeros, so repetition cannot begin. This is an explicit construction illustrating the criterion for irrationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2.1.1 — Sequence as function from ℕ to ℝ
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of real numbers is a function x: ℕ → ℝ. The nth element is denoted x_n; the sequence is often written (x_n)_{n=1}^∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation comments: sometimes written {x_n}_{n=1}^∞ or x_1, x_2, ...; distinction between sequence and the set/range of its values is emphasized with examples (e.g., constant sequence vs set of values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded sequence (definition embedded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n)_{n=1}^∞ is bounded if there exists B ∈ ℝ such that |x_n| ≤ B for all n ∈ ℕ (similarly bounded above/below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1/n is bounded (B=1); the natural numbers sequence 1,2,3,... is not bounded. Use this to check convergence prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2.1.2 — Convergence (epsilon–M definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n) converges to x ∈ ℝ if for every ε > 0 there exists M ∈ ℕ such that |x_n - x| < ε for all n ≥ M. Notation: lim_{n→∞} x_n = x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key pedagogical point: M may depend on ε. Convergent = converges to some x; divergent otherwise. Examples given (constant sequence, 1/n → 0) and nonexamples (alternating sequence 1,-1,1,-1,...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.1.6 — Uniqueness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A convergent sequence has a unique limit: if lim x_n = x and lim x_n = y then x = y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: given ε>0, pick M1,M2 for x and y, pick n≥max(M1,M2) and apply triangle inequality to show |x-y| < ε for arbitrary ε, hence x=y. This illustrates a common analysis technique of splitting quantities and estimating each by small numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.1.7 — Convergent sequences are bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n) converges to x then (x_n) is bounded: there exists B with |x_n| ≤ B for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: choose M so that for n ≥ M, |x_n - x| < 1, then finitely many initial terms form a finite set; take maximum of their absolute values and the bound from the tail. Counterexample note: boundedness alone does not imply convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2.1.9 and Theorem 2.1.10 — Monotone sequences and Monotone Convergence Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence is monotone increasing if x_n ≤ x_{n+1} for all n (monotone decreasing analogously). The Monotone Convergence Theorem: a monotone sequence converges iff it is bounded. Moreover, if (x_n) is monotone increasing and bounded then lim x_n = sup{x_n: n ∈ ℕ}; if monotone decreasing and bounded then lim x_n = inf{x_n: n ∈ ℕ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: for increasing bounded sequence let x = sup; find M with x_M > x - ε and use monotonicity to show tail sits within ε of x. Practical usage: checking monotonicity + boundedness often suffices to prove convergence and identify the limit (sup/inf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2.1.14 and Proposition 2.1.15 — Tail of a sequence and independence of initial terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The K-tail of (x_n) is the subsequence starting at index K: (x_{n+K})_{n=1}^∞. Convergence of a sequence depends only on its tails: (x_n) converges iff some (equivalently every) K-tail converges, and the limits are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: one may discard finitely many initial terms when testing convergence. Useful when a sequence becomes monotone or otherwise better-behaved after some index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 2.1.16 and Proposition 2.1.17 — Subsequences and limits of subsequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequence is (x_{n_i}) where n_i is strictly increasing. If (x_n) converges to x then every subsequence converges to x. Existence of different convergent subsequences with different limits implies the original sequence is divergent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tail is a special subsequence. Examples: alternating 0,1,0,1,... has subsequences converging to 0 and 1; hence the original diverges. Exercises explore sequences having subsequences converging to every real number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.2.1 — Squeeze (Sandwich) lemma for sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If sequences a_n ≤ x_n ≤ b_n for all n, and lim a_n = lim b_n = L, then lim x_n = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof by choosing M where tails of a_n and b_n are within ε of L and using inequalities. Example: use constant sequences as bounds to show certain decaying sequences go to 0 (e.g., 1/(n√n) ≤ 1/n → 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.2.3 and Corollary 2.2.4 — Limits preserve non-strict inequalities and bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n ≤ y_n for all n and both converge, then lim x_n ≤ lim y_n. If a ≤ x_n ≤ b for all n and x_n converges, then a ≤ lim x_n ≤ b. Note: strict inequalities need not be preserved in the limit (x_n < y_n ∀n does not imply lim x_n < lim y_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: apply the epsilon definition to both sequences and add inequalities. Warning/example provided: sequences approaching 0 show strict inequality can become non-strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.2.5 — Algebra of limits (sum, difference, scalar multiple, product, quotient)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n and y_n converge to x and y respectively then: lim (x_n + y_n) = x + y; lim (x_n - y_n) = x - y; lim (c x_n) = c x for constant c; lim (x_n y_n) = x y; and if lim y_n ≠ 0 and y_n ≠ 0 for all n then lim (x_n / y_n) = x / y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use triangle inequality and bounding arguments; the quotient case reduces to proving lim 1/y_n = 1/lim y_n when denom limit is nonzero (a claim proved by bounding denominators away from zero on the tail). Practical note: must ensure denominator sequence does not approach zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.2.6 — Limits pass through roots (kth root)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n) converges to x and x_n ≥ 0 for all n and x ≥ 0, then lim √{x_n} = √{x}. More generally, the kth root limit holds for kth roots under analogous nonnegativity conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses algebraic manipulation and earlier algebra-of-limits results; requires showing x_n close to x implies √{x_n} close to √{x}, with separate small- and positive-limit cases handled. One must ensure nonnegativity to take real roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.2.7 — Limit commutes with absolute value
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n converges to x then lim |x_n| = |x|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via reverse triangle inequality: ||x_n| - |x|| ≤ |x_n - x|, so making |x_n - x| small makes ||x_n| - |x|| small. Use this to deduce limit behavior of absolute-valued sequences; note converse need not hold (|x_n| → 0 does not imply x_n → 0? actually it does, but other converses may fail as exercise 2.1.7 suggests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for recursively defined sequences and Newton's method example
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sequence is defined recursively (x_{n+1} = F(x_n)), standard steps: (1) show sequence is well-defined (no division by zero, iterates exist), (2) show boundedness and monotonicity (often by induction), (3) conclude convergence (e.g., monotone + bounded), (4) take limit on both sides to obtain algebraic equation for the limit. Example: x_{n+1} = (x_n + 2/x_n)/2 with x_1 = 2 (Newton iteration) is shown positive, monotone decreasing and bounded below, hence convergent to √2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: use induction to show positivity; show monotonicity by manipulating inequality x_{n+1} ≤ x_n; boundedness follows from positivity; taking limits yields fixed-point equation x = (x + 2/x)/2 ⇒ x^2 = 2 ⇒ x = √2 (positive root). Cautions: verify assumptions (e.g., denominators nonzero) before taking limits.
